young.html: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe (say GUR-tuh) was Germany's most famous poet. He worked on one play, Faust, for about sixty years, from when he was a young man until just before he died.

Faust is a scholar who has read every book in his study and still feels he knows nothing important. A clever devil named Mephistopheles (say meff-ih-STOFF-uh-leez) offers him a deal: he will show Faust every pleasure in the world. Faust makes a bet: if he ever finds a moment so wonderful that he wants it to last forever, he will lose.

Faust goes on many adventures, makes terrible mistakes, and hurts people he loves. But he keeps striving, and at the very end he finds his happiest moment not in pleasure but in planning work that will help many people live freely. And, in Goethe's version, he is saved.

young.html: For parents: Part One includes the tragedy of Gretchen, which involves adult themes. The lesson summarizes it gently. Young readers can enjoy the opening scenes and the idea of the wager, or a retelling.

The moment you'd keep. Faust is looking for one perfect moment. Draw or write about a moment you wish could have lasted forever. What made it special? Was it something you got, or something you did or shared?

full.html: Goethe (1749–1832) was a poet, novelist, scientist and statesman at the small court of Weimar. The Faust legend, a German tale of a scholar who sells his soul for knowledge and power, was already old; Christopher Marlowe had made it a play in the 1590s, and Goethe saw it as a puppet show as a boy. He began his own version in the 1770s, published Part One in 1808, and finished Part Two in 1831; it appeared in 1832, after his death. Bayard Taylor's English translation (1870–71) keeps Goethe's rhymes and meters.

full.text:
I've studied now Philosophy
And Jurisprudence, Medicine,—
And even, alas! Theology,—
From end to end, with labor keen;
And here, poor fool! with all my lore
I stand, no wiser than before

full.ed: Houghton, Mifflin and Company, Boston (1882 printing)

full.html: The play opens with a Prologue in Heaven, modeled on the Book of Job: Mephistopheles asks to tempt Faust, and the Lord allows it, confident that "a good man, through obscurest aspiration, / Has still an instinct of the one true way." Faust, in despair, turns to magic, and Mephistopheles comes to him, first as a black poodle.

full.text:
FAUST. ... Who art thou, then?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Part of that Power, not understood,
Which always wills the Bad, and always works the Good.
full.author: Goethe
full.ed: Houghton, Mifflin and Company, Boston (1882 printing)

full.text:
When thus I hail the Moment flying:
"Ah, still delay—thou art so fair!"
Then bind me in thy bonds undying,
My final ruin then declare!
full.author: Goethe
full.work: Faust, Part One, the Study (Scene IV)
full.ed: Houghton, Mifflin and Company, Boston (1882 printing)

full.html: The wager changes the old legend. Marlowe's Faustus sells his soul for twenty-four years of power. Goethe's Faust bets that nothing Mephistopheles offers will ever satisfy his restless striving. The question of the play is whether striving itself is Faust's curse or his salvation.

full.html: The heart of Part One is the story of Gretchen (Margaret), a pious young townswoman whom Faust loves and, with Mephistopheles' help, pursues. Their love brings ruin on her family, and she is condemned for a terrible act done in despair. In the last scene Faust tries to rescue her from prison; she refuses to escape with him and gives herself to God's judgment. Mephistopheles cries that she is judged; a voice from above answers, "She is saved."

full.html: Part Two is a vast symbolic pageant through politics, money, ancient Greece and science. At the end, old and blind, Faust plans to drain a marsh so that free people can live on new land. Imagining that, he says the fatal words and dies. But angels carry off his immortal part, singing:

full.html: Thinking Faust is simply a warning against ambition. Goethe's play judges Faust harshly for the harm he does, yet ends in mercy for a man who never stopped striving. Readers still argue about whether that ending is just.

items: The Book of Job and Dante's Comedy: Goethe's Prologue echoes Job, and his ending, with Gretchen among the blessed leading Faust upward, echoes Beatrice in the Paradiso.
Marlowe's Doctor Faustus (1590s) ends in damnation; Goethe's ends in redemption.
Milton's Satan and Goethe's Mephistopheles are two great portraits of evil, one grand, one witty and mocking.
Later, "Faustian" became a word for a restless hunger for knowledge and power at any cost.
Is never being satisfied a good thing or a bad thing?
Can someone who does great harm still be forgiven? Who decides?
Why does the devil say he "works the Good" without meaning to?
What kind of moment would truly be worth asking to stay?

questions: Faust read every book and still felt empty. What do you think he was missing?
Why do you think Goethe let Faust be saved, when the old story ended in punishment?
Is it ever wise to make a bet about your own happiness?
Faust's happiest moment came from planning work that helps others. Why might that be more satisfying than fun?
What would you warn Faust about, if you could talk to him at the start?
